5f44981219915071: KUALA LUMPUR, Sept 29 — As strata properties become an increasingly common choice for homebuyers, owning one involves more than paying a mortgage and maintenance fees.

While a new home may be your own, living in a strata development means not everything is entirely up to you. Residents are expected to abide by rules, commonly known as by-laws, governing how they use their units, facilities and common spaces.
The law behind strata by-laws

For those unfamiliar with them, these rules form part of the broader legal framework governing strata properties in Peninsular Malaysia and the Federal Territory of Labuan under the Strata Management Act 2013 (SMA).
Sarawak has its own Strata Management Ordinance 2019.
Sabah, meanwhile, passed the Building Management Enactment 2026, although it has yet to come into force.
In essence, the SMA provides for the management and maintenance of strata buildings and their common property, while setting out the rights and responsibilities of homeowners and management bodies.

Section 150 empowers the minister, after consultation with the National Council for Local Government, to make regulations for the implementation of the Act, including on the proper maintenance and management of buildings and common property.
What the standard by-laws cover

Because by-laws play a vital role in regulating daily life in a strata community, the Third Schedule of the Strata Management (Maintenance and Management) Regulations 2015 sets out 30 by-laws across eight parts.
Made under the SMA, these by-laws provide a standardised set of rules for strata properties in Peninsular Malaysia and the Federal Territory of Labuan.
They cover everyday issues residents may encounter, including nuisance, pets, vehicles, common facilities, security and unpaid charges.

Under the by-laws governing nuisance, for example, noise from electrical or electronic equipment, appliances or musical instruments used within a parcel or on common property must be kept at a low volume after 11pm to avoid disturbing other proprietors, unless prior written approval has been obtained.

For pet owners, the by-laws prohibit keeping animals in a parcel or on common property if they cause a nuisance or annoyance, pose a risk to the safety or health of other residents, or breach state or local authority laws and regulations.
For vehicles, improperly parked or unauthorised vehicles may be towed or wheel-clamped at the owner’s expense without prior notice.

Vehicle owners must also ensure their alarms are properly maintained to prevent frequent false alarms that could annoy other residents. Management may prohibit a vehicle from entering the development for a specified period if its alarm repeatedly causes a nuisance.

On security, management may require anyone on the common property to identify themselves and, if they refuse and are not a proprietor, require them to leave the common property or development area immediately.
The rules also give management certain powers when charges remain unpaid.
Management may display the names of proprietors with outstanding payments, along with their parcel details and the amount owed, on notice boards in the building. The list must be updated monthly.

It may also, after 14 days have passed from the defaulter receiving the relevant notice and without further notice, deactivate an electromagnetic access device — such as an access card or tag — until the outstanding sum is paid.
Management may also stop or suspend a defaulter from using common facilities or services, including a car park bay on common property designated for the defaulter’s use.
Buildings can set additional rules
The statutory by-laws are not necessarily the end of the story.

Under the SMA, a joint management body or management corporation may, by special resolution, introduce additional by-laws or amend existing additional by-laws, provided they are not inconsistent with the prescribed by-laws.
These may regulate matters including:
safety and security measures;
restrictions on the use of common property;
the keeping of pets;
parking;
floor coverings;
refuse control;
behaviour;
architectural and landscaping guidelines; and
fines of up to RM200 for a proprietor, occupant or invitee who breaches the by-laws.

For example, additional by-laws may introduce more detailed conditions governing pets, such as limits based on size or rules on where animals may be taken, provided those rules are consistent with the statutory by-laws.
They may also introduce stricter security requirements for visitors, such as requiring more detailed identification or documentation than the standard registration process.

That is why two buildings operating under the same statutory framework can still feel quite different from day to day: one may allow motorcycles in visitor bays while another may not; one may specify renovation hours while another imposes broader restrictions.
Can I challenge a by-law?
The short answer is yes.
Additional by-laws must comply with the SMA and cannot be inconsistent with the prescribed statutory by-laws.

The Strata Management Tribunal has jurisdiction over certain disputes involving by-laws and resolutions, including claims seeking to revoke amendments to by-laws, while the SMA also allows a management body or parcel owner or proprietor, as applicable, to seek orders from the Tribunal or a court to enforce a by-law, restrain a breach or recover damages arising from one.
Homeowners may also raise concerns over proposed or existing additional by-laws through their development’s general meeting process.
726246b46d23e2b3: Jakarta, Sept 29 — For weeks, Indonesia has been battling fires that have burned vast swathes of forest and peat ecosystems, causing toxic haze to blanket parts of the country, Malaysia and Singapore.
The fires have harmed humans and animals alike, and prompted criminal charges, license suspensions and a presidentially mandated new agency to tackle fires in peat ecosystems.
Here’s what to know:
What is the latest situation?

Between January and July alone, more than 202,000 hectares were razed by fire, according to government figures. That is an area roughly three times the size of the capital Jakarta, and represents a 69-per cent increase in burned areas in the same period last year.
But the figures have not been updated since, and the burning has only worsened.
The Nusantara Atlas project, which uses satellite monitoring, estimates nearly 896,000 hectares — over five times the size of Greater London — had burned by the end of August.
South Papua province on the country’s easternmost island was the most-affected region, with over 168,000 hectares burned as of August, according to Nusantara Atlas.
NGO Yayasan Pusaka Bentala Rakyat said fires have been detected inside a large-scale government food estate project in South Papua, local media reported.
What is causing the fires?
The El Nino weather phenomenon typically brings dry conditions to Indonesia, and this cycle is predicted to be among the strongest in decades and last until early 2027.
But experts said human factors are also key, including slash-and-burn land-clearing and decades of forest degradation that have changed the naturally fire-resistant landscape.
“El Nino isn’t actually the cause, but it’s a trigger. There still needs to be an ignitor,” IPB University forestry lecturer Ati Dwi Nurhayati told AFP.
“We know that in peatlands, almost 100 per cent (of the fires) was caused by human activity.”

Peat ecosystems are dense layers of partially decomposed organic materials that are normally waterlogged. But in much of Indonesia they have been dried out so the land can be planted. This created highly flammable regions.
Once peat catches fire, it can smoulder and reignite for days, making firefighting efforts complex.
In the first eight months of this year, over 212,000 hotspots have been detected inside peat ecosystems across the country, according to NGO Pantau Gambut.
The figure was more than double that recorded during 2015’s strong El Nino.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Members of the all-women The Power of Mama (TPoM) volunteer firefighting team spray water onto smouldering peatland in Mensubuk Lama, Tanjungpura Village, Ketapang Regency, West Kalimantan on September 26, 2026. — AFP pic
What is the government’s response?
Indonesia has deployed firefighters assisted by volunteers across affected areas, and used cloud-seeding and water-bombing, with limited success. Malaysia and Japan have also offered assistance.
Authorities revoked the permits of five companies accused of contributed to the fires, with dozens more frozen.
President Prabowo Subianto last week ordered the creation of a new government agency to manage tropical peat and mangrove ecosystems and carry out fire prevention.
Indonesia set up a similar agency after the 2015 fires, initially tasked with peat and expanded to mangroves in 2020. But its mandate was not renewed when it expired in 2024.
In 2015, fires burned more than two million hectares in Indonesia, costing an estimated US$16.1 billion in damages, according to the World Bank.
But the agency’s establishment has been met with some scepticism.

“The important thing is to ensure that this agency’s mandate can answer the issue of peat management, not just introduce a new structure,” Pantau Gambut senior campaigner Putra Saptian said in a statement.
What are the impacts?
Indonesia’s health ministry said last week that cases of respiratory illness have climbed past 170,000 in haze-hit provinces across Sumatra and Borneo.
The blazes have also had a devastating impact on wildlife.
Indonesian authorities have rescued 100 animals, including 53 orangutans, that were threatened by the blazes, a forestry ministry official said last week.
In Borneo, fires have been detected within habitats containing 52 per cent of the island’s orangutan population, the International Union for Conservation of Nature said.
The haze has spread beyond Indonesia’s border, drifting particularly into Malaysian Borneo’s Sarawak state where schools have periodically closed because of the smog.
It has also reached Singapore and even caused declining air quality in the Philippines and southern Thailand. — AFP
c0ee2d8a9fed40e9: BEIJING, Sept 29 — Watching Sha Ma Laqian perform stunts atop a stack of chairs reaching up to 10 metres, it may seem effortless for him, but the feat is the culmination of 12 years of training that began in childhood.

The 19-year-old youth — a member of the Yi ethnic group, one of China’s minority communities — is part of China’s Sichuan Suining Acrobatics Troupe, which performed a series of nine acts in the one-hour Legend of Chinese Charm show at the Beijing Chaoyang Theatre here last Friday.

Among the audience were participants of the Asean Media Workshop in China, including Bernama, who had the opportunity to gain first-hand exposure to the country’s traditional performing arts and cultural heritage.
Laqian said he began learning acrobatics at the age of seven and that continuous training helped him to improve his skills and overcome nervousness when performing the high-chair act.
“When I first started performing this act, I was quite nervous, but after doing it repeatedly, I no longer feel nervous,” he told the media after the performance.

He said the skills for the high-chair routine he performed at the show require years of training, beginning with basic movements before progressing to more difficult acts. It took him about eight to nine years to reach his current level of proficiency.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Sha Ma Laqian said he began learning acrobatics at the age of seven and that continuous training helped him to improve his skills and overcome nervousness when performing the high-chair act. — Bernama pic
However, mastering the art has not been without challenges as he has sustained injuries during training and performances.
“Injuries are common in the field of acrobatics, but the applause and encouragement from the audience make all the effort to learn and improve in this art worthwhile,” he said.
During Friday’s performance, Laqian performed at a height of about 10 metres, while his highest record so far is 14 metres.

By performing in such shows, he hopes to introduce and showcase Chinese acrobatics to the international community, allowing more people around the world to discover the uniqueness and beauty of the art.

He added that the costume he wore incorporates elements of traditional Chinese culture and was designed in the “Shusheng” style, depicting the image of a traditional Chinese scholar or student in line with the theme of the performance.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

The Legend of Chinese Charm show featured more than 60 performers. The audience was clearly captivated by the various acrobatic acts performed by the artistes, who showcased their skills, strength, balance and artistry of traditional Chinese acrobatics, supported by modern stage technology. Each act drew thunderous applause.

Apart from the high-chair act, in which Laqian participated, the show also featured plate spinning, bowl balancing and hat juggling acts; ground ring acrobatics; bicycle acrobatics; and a flying motorcycle show.
The performance was among the cultural programmes attended by the participants of the Asean Media Workshop.

For the media practitioners, the showcase also offered a glimpse into how traditional Chinese acrobatics continue to be presented through contemporary stage productions, combining physical skills and traditional performance elements with modern stage technology to engage today’s audiences.
The two-week Asean Media Workshop, which started on September 15, involved 21 journalists from nine countries, with the programme also covering visits to Nanning, Fujian and Beijing. — Bernama
502693a2972b8ff2: WASHINGTON, Sept 29 — It bills itself as an “independent journalism” outfit, but the innocuous-sounding North Carolinian is among hundreds of partisan sites that researchers say masquerade as local news outlets in battleground states ahead of the US midterm elections.

The so-called “pink slime” sites — many secretly backed by partisan groups on both sides of the political aisle — appear to be fuelling an explosion of polarising or false narratives ahead of the November 3 elections.

Their backers are splurging hundreds of thousands of dollars on advertising their articles on social media, expanding their otherwise limited readership while authentic media outlets grapple with financial woes, layoffs, and record low public trust.

The Senate Leadership Fund (SLF), a political action committee that describes itself as “solely dedicated to protecting and expanding the Republican Senate majority,” apparently launched the North Carolinian in July, according to disinformation watchdog NewsGuard.
The North Carolinian said the site was “paid for by SLF” and was “not authorised by any candidate or candidate’s committee.”

But the site appears focused on opposing Democrat Roy Cooper’s campaign for US Senate and boosting his Republican opponent in the southern state, Michael Whatley. It carries headlines with phrases such as, “Roy Cooper’s disastrous crime record” and “Whatley highlights Democrat Cooper’s dangerous soft-on-crime record.”
SLF spent between US$34,700 and US$46,715 (RM141,766 and RM190,854) promoting the site’s articles on Meta platforms through late August, garnering at least 3.6 million views, according to NewsGuard.
SLF did not respond to AFP’s request for comment.
‘Undermining trust’

“Pink slime” outlets — some suspected of using AI tools to produce their articles — have proliferated in recent years, outnumbering American newspaper sites, in a trend that experts say is eroding trust in traditional media.

NewsGuard has identified 21 pink slime outlets that launched this year, bringing the total number of such sites to 1,179. By comparison, only 937 daily newspapers were operating, according to Northwestern University’s Local News Initiative.

“These pink slime sites can be confounding to news consumers who may not be aware of their agendas and confuse them with authentic independent news websites in their area, thereby undermining trust between journalists and their readers of all political persuasions,” said NewsGuard’s Sam Howard.

NewsGuard said two pink slime networks — One Nation on the right, and the American Independent on the left — collectively spent at least US$801,500 on advertising in the first eight months of this year to promote their articles on Facebook and Instagram.
Their growing online reach could potentially affect the responses of AI chatbots, which are now popularly used for online searches, researchers say.

One Nation, an affiliate of SLF, has launched six sites posing as independent news portals in states with key Senate races — Georgia, Alaska, Maine, Iowa, Ohio, and New Hampshire — according to the independent newsletter Popular Information.
One Nation is “producing propaganda masquerading as journalism,” the newsletter said.
The American Independent and One Nation did not respond to an AFP request for comment.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

People vote on the second day of early voting ahead of the midterm elections, at a polling place at DuPage Event Center and Fairgrounds in Wheaton, Illinois, on September 25, 2026. NewsGuard said two pink slime networks — One Nation on the right, and the American Independent on the left — collectively spent at least US$801,500 on advertising in the first eight months of this year to promote their articles on Facebook and Instagram. — AFP pic
‘Tricked’
The sites are dubbed “pink slime” after the fluorescent pink meat paste used as an additive by food manufacturers.
In the age of cheap, widely available AI tools, producing and circulating their content — described as “pseudo-journalism” by the Columbia Journalism Review — has never been easier.

Last year, a study supported by Yale University’s Institution for Social and Policy Studies warned of their growing influence, saying many users often prefer such sites over traditional media adhering to ethical practices.

“These sites seem to take money from campaigns or political operatives and write pieces that are biased or have some sort of angle, with this veneer of a legitimate news site,” said Kevin DeLuca, an assistant professor of political science at the university.
“Such sites have the potential for making people believe things that are not true without understanding where the information is coming from.”
The rise of pink slime comes amid a rapid decline of local newspapers, many of which have either shut down or suffered extensive layoffs due to economic headwinds.

Last year, Northwestern University identified over 212 counties out of some 3,000 in the United States as “news deserts,” having no locally-based news sources such as newspapers and public radio. — AFP
a6e2e811c990a751: PAJU (South Korea), Sept 29 — A building-sized North Korean flag waves from a tower on the de facto border with South Korea, marking territory that experts say has become nearly impossible to escape.
The combined total of North Koreans to reach South Korea in the past six years is less than the number that typically defected each year for decades — and appears to be declining further in 2026.
The main cause is leader Kim Jong Un’s aim to preserve his family dynasty by sealing the country off from the outside, keeping people in and information out, experts say.
“As I understand it, bringing family members directly from North Korea is currently impossible,” 29-year-old Chae Yoon-seo, who fled in 2019, told AFP.
She swam across a river into China at night with a smuggler’s help, and travelled through Laos, Vietnam and Thailand before finally flying to South Korea.
Defections to the South hit a peak of more than 2,900 in 2009 and stayed well above 1,000 per year for the next decade.
But there were just 63 in the first half of this year — down by over a third from the same period in 2025, said Seoul’s Unification Ministry.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

In this file photo taken on October 4, 2022, UNC (United Nations Command) soldiers (right) and a South Korean soldier (left) stand guard before North Korea's Panmon Hall (rear C) and the military demarcation line separating North and South Korea, at Panmunjom, in the Joint Security Area (JSA) of the Demilitarised Zone (DMZ). Twenty-five years ago, a desperate director risked jail to make a movie about an unlikely friendship between North and South Korean soldiers, striking box office gold and launching his actors to global stardom today. — AFP pic
‘Soviet-style border’
Arrivals have fluctuated over the decades, but plunged sharply during the Covid pandemic when many nations shut their borders.
A key change in North Korea, however, started years before.
After taking power in 2011, Kim began restricting the informal trade and migration links along the roughly 1,415-kilometre (880-mile) northern border with China.
In addition to being an economic lifeline, the Chinese border region has also been the first step in most defectors’ escapes.
The long frontier was relatively porous, unlike the heavily mined, fenced and surveilled Demilitarised Zone (DMZ) that serves as the Koreas’ de facto border.
Along the boundary with China, Kim’s government has erected fences and installed cameras as well as strips of sand that preserve the footprints of anyone who crosses.
“North Koreans built a real Soviet-style border security system,” said Andrei Lankov, an expert on the North at Kookmin University in Seoul.
Beijing has helped too, said Lankov, noting China’s preference to keep the status quo of the Kim dynasty by opposing potential instability from defectors or their supporters.
As part of its efforts, China reportedly has put in place hundreds of facial recognition cameras, noted Rachel Minyoung Lee, senior fellow with the Stimson Centre’s 38 North.
She added that Beijing also added more patrol boats and new or planned deportation facilities along its northeastern border.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

A North Korean defector (centre) living in South Korea holds a placard reading ‘Recognise North Korean refugees!’ during a rally calling to stop China’s forced repatriation of North Korean defectors in front of the Chinese embassy in Seoul September 22, 2026. — AFP pic
Ousted, killed or exiled
The roughly 34,500 defectors to reach the South since 1998 are a fraction of North Korea’s 26.6 million people, UN figures show, but the plunging number of escapes has consequences.
“Defectors are the main source of information about the North,” said Fyodor Tertitsky, lecturer at Seoul’s Korea University, noting both South Korean intelligence and researchers interrogate them.
Though some people still do get out.
Defector Gyuri Kang’s 2023 escape by boat with her mother and aunt — across the maritime border with the South, an extremely rare feat — was a “miracle”, she told a UN hearing.
She is also a case in point for why North Korea has made great efforts to seal itself off.
Kang noted the influence of South Korean dramas smuggled in on USB drives, finding them “so refreshing and more credible than North Korea state propaganda”.
“North Korean authorities are keenly aware of the impact of outside media,” she said.
In 2020, North Korea made possessing foreign media a crime punishable by years-long forced labour terms—and potential death sentences for large-scale distribution, according to Amnesty International.
Lankov, from Kookmin University, said external information is the greatest threat to the long-term survival of North Korea’s leadership.
“If they let their people interact with the outside world, they are highly likely to be overthrown, and maybe killed or driven into exile,” he added.
Chae, the defector, said her hope was that the North’s isolated people are not one day simply forgotten by the outside world.
“These days, there are a lot of cynical reactions on helping other countries, so I am a bit worried that one day, interest in North Korean human rights might fade away as well,” she added. — AFP
f3e6bee3fd00ef36: WASHINGTON, Sept 29 — Donald Trump could become a lame duck president after US midterm elections but prospects at the ballot box are looking brighter for ducks of the feathered variety.

When Washington DC residents vote in the November 3 congressional elections, with Trump’s Republican Party forecast to fare poorly, there will be an additional measure on the ballot: to ban the sale and distribution in the city of foie gras.

Animal rights activists collected the signatures of five per cent of registered voters in the District of Colombia to mandate the referendum on the quintessentially French culinary delicacy that is made from the enlarged duck livers.

“They put a rod in a duck’s throat to make its liver get bigger. That’s not cool,” said campaign volunteer James Nance, referring to force feeding of fowl, as he stapled “Save the ducks” signs on lampposts on a busy uptown street.
Advocates are confident the measure will pass, although, as with a lot of politics in the nation’s capital, the debate on “Initiative 86” is rancorous.
The proposal — echoing the restaurant shorthand “86” for an item that is off the menu — pits zealous reformers against vested interests, with an electorate knowing little about the issue.
The most prominent opponent is Bart Hutchins, chef and owner of Butterworth’s, an upscale restaurant near Capitol Hill popular with Trump administration officials and supporters.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
A photograph shows slices of foie gras on the first day of the national duck vaccination campaign, in Labarthete, southwestern France September 2, 2023. — AFP pic
Foie gras is his favourite ingredient and a fixture on his menu — used in his tartare presentation, to mount sauces, as a pate, and even for ice cream.
Hutchins is pessimistic about staving off the ban and laments what it would mean for the city’s famed French restaurants.
“It’s this very modern thing where we just kind of keep throwing away the past,” Hutchins said.
“Next year it’ll be banning something else relatively small...until we’re all just eating, you know, chicken nuggets, and we’ll have no culinary heritage whatsoever.”
For the activists at Pro Animal DC, who are seeking to emulate places like California and Pittsburgh that have enacted laws against foie gras, it’s about fighting animal cruelty.

“DC is actually the third top consumer of foie gras in the entire country. So getting this cruel product out of DC would have a really big impact on the foie gras industry,” group spokeswoman Natalie Fulton said.
They gathered nearly 32,000 verified signatures to get “Initiative 86” on the ballot, which is more signatures than for a proposal to legalise cannabis approved in 2014.
They see voter ignorance as the main obstacle.
“A lot of people don’t know what it is, and that’s I think why it’s been allowed for so long, despite how cruel it is,” said activist and tech worker Mike Accardi.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
An employee feeds a duck at Hudson Valley Foie Gras in Ferndale, New York March 3, 2023. — AFP pic
Who decides the menu?
Jordan Grinor, director at one of only two US commercial foie gras producers, Hudson Valley Farms, strongly disputes the charge of cruelty.
He said that in the wild, ducks gorge before migration and store fat in their livers and argues that “gavage” — the process of force-feeding — is a traditional means of animal husbandry.

“Should governments have the power to say what we’re allowed to eat? That’s really the question here,” he said, adding that a DC ban could put at least a third of his 150 foie gras employees out of work in upstate New York.

The economic impact on Washington restaurants would probably be less marked, but Hutchins — who last year faced a social media barrage in the liberal city for hosting Trump luminaries at Butterworth’s — voiced disappointment that more of his gastronomic competitors are not speaking out against the proposed ban.
“A lot of chefs are being very quiet about this, and I understand that because they’re sort of scared of the protesters,” he said.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
An employee processes duck at Hudson Valley Foie Gras in Ferndale, New York March 3, 2023. — AFP pic
Meat, yes. Foie Gras? No

The amiable campaigners AFP accompanied on a recent sign-posting spree on Washington’s uptown Georgia Avenue, did not match the profile of angry activists. They included two vegans and unusually, a dedicated carnivore.
Nance, a lawyer who regularly posts pictures of his favourite meat dishes on Instagram, is definitely in a minority in a heavily vegetarian movement, but says it’s worth campaigning for.

“There are more pressing issues like defence of democracy, like standing up to the (Trump) administration’s encroachments on democracy” but since the ban is on the ballot, “I figured I might as well help out.” — AFP

THE Health Ministry is stepping up preventive measures and strengthening school-based mental health support to address suicidal behaviour among students, particularly where bullying is a factor.

Minister Datuk Seri Dr Dzulkefly Ahmad said the ministry was working with the Education Ministry to improve counselling services, early detection and intervention for students showing signs of distress.

"We are carrying out various awareness and literacy activities to raise awareness on this issue," he said after launching the national-level World Self-harm Prevention Day, themed "Change the Narrative, Ignite Hope" at the Kolej Poly-Tech Mara in Meru.
Dzulkefly said the government had also launched the national anti-bullying policy, which provided a framework for efforts to address bullying and strengthen support for those affected.
He said counselling services in schools would be strengthened to include screening, early detection of behavioural changes and early intervention.
"This is important. We want to ensure that issues are detected early and that appropriate support is provided."
Dzulkefly said the ministry would also deploy its Mental Health and Psychosocial Support Services team to assist affected students, schools and communities.
He said the team would conduct interventions and outreach programmes based on the needs of those affected.
"The School Health Programme is also important, particularly in terms of mental health literacy and awareness."
He said the ministry aimed to create a more inclusive and positive school environment that will enable students to develop healthy coping mechanisms and resilience.
Dzulkefly added that strategic risk communication was important, especially when addressing suicidal behaviour, as such issues must be communicated carefully and sensitively.
He said inaccurate or poorly handled communication could have unintended negative consequences.
He stressed that addressing suicidal behaviour among students also required the cooperation of multiple agencies.
44c756e4ef2cdc18: NEW YORK: US prosecutors reopened an investigation Monday into an alleged gang rape at Cornell University following claims the elite college failed to properly punish the men involved.
The alleged victim said in a civil lawsuit this month she was drugged with ketamine, assaulted and raped in 2024 by seven members of the Chi Phi fraternity, a social club for male students.
Cornell closed the fraternity and temporarily suspended the students involved, several of whom were later expelled.
The newly released details of the alleged incident have fuelled allegations that the university was too lenient and reignited a debate over sexual assault on US campuses.
Matthew Van Houten, district attorney for Tompkins County in New York, said that he plans to file criminal charges against the seven men.
He said his office chose in 2024 not to prosecute because the victim's testimony did not establish a lack of consent but had now decided to do so in light of her latest allegations.
"I recognise the reality that it can take years of therapy and healing for victims of sexual assaults to fully process and understand what happened to them," Van Houten said in a statement.
"Seeking justice sometimes requires us to reconsider or reopen cases when we are provided with additional evidence."
Kyle Kimball, vice president of university relations at Cornell, said the Ivy League school supports the decision to reinvestigate the case.
He also rejected a claim, made in the civil lawsuit, that the suspects were offered the opportunity to write essays to mitigate their conduct.
"Any suggestion that the university did not impose consequential punishments for those involved is false," Kimball said.
The 101-page civil lawsuit filed in New York gives graphic details on the alleged assault of the woman, whose identity is being protected.
Notably, it provides a screenshot of a Snapchat group message advertising "free pussy" during the incident, apparently an invitation for other fraternity members to take part.
The suit seeks financial damages from Cornell and the seven suspects, adding that the woman has suffered "severe emotional and psychological distress".
British actor Florence Pugh has voiced her anger about the case, saying she felt "uneasy and sick and anxious" after hearing about it.
"Colleges/schools/universities repeatedly fail women around the world," she wrote on Instagram.
"You build men that get taught through time and time again that they can do extreme harm and that they won't be harmed in return," Pugh said.
Prominent Democratic lawmaker Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez condemned a "culture of rape" at elite institutions like Cornell.
"Jane Doe, that survivor, lost her education because you can't stay in school when something like that happens to you," Ocasio-Cortez said Sunday.
"She had to lose her education, and those men were protected by an institution and granted an Ivy League degree as a reward. Never again."
ae399fbf45b314a4: METZ, France: Pope Leo XIV warned on Monday that relations between nations were becoming increasingly uncivilised with people boasting of "lies and deceit", urging Europe to help break the spiral and foster respect in international ties.

Speaking in the city of Metz near the border with Germany where he was wrapping up a four-day visit to France, the leader of the world's 1.4 billion Catholics did not mention any world leaders by name.
The pope sees Europe as a counterweight to major powers and has in the past called on the European Union to overcome tensions and rediscover unity in pursuit of peace in Ukraine and beyond.
Leo, the first US pontiff, has clashed with President Donald Trump in recent months over the harsh crackdown on immigration in the United States and the war on Iran.

"Relations between individuals and states are becoming increasingly uncivilised. The value of keeping one's word is dismissed. Instead, people boast of lies and deceit," Leo said in French, alongside President Emmanuel Macron and a handful of other leaders.
"Europe can help to break this cycle through the respect for others that it has learned to cultivate and preserve," Leo said, on the first official papal visit to France in nearly two decades.

Metz, which changed hands between France and Germany in past conflicts, is associated with Robert Schuman, considered one of the founding fathers of the European Union, who is buried just outside the city.
Throughout his trip, the pope has appeared smiling and warm, readily engaging with crowds.
"We are very pleased to have a pope who dares to take a political stand," said Isabelle Gerber, a Protestant pastor.

On Monday morning, the pontiff, who is passionate about aviation, spent half an hour in the cockpit of the Air France plane that flew him to Metz and also blessed the crews of the Rafale fighter jets escorting his aircraft.
In his speech, Leo urged "courage in negotiation" and compromise to put an end to war on the continent, in an apparent reference to Russia's war against Ukraine, now in its fifth year.
"Sadly, war has returned, even to Europe," he said.
"We need to commit ourselves to patient dialogue, to show courage in negotiation and to be willing to give up some positions for the greater good of peace."
Vladimir Putin has shown little readiness to negotiate an end to the war against Ukraine.
Leo appealed for unity as nationalist movements are gaining strength in Europe. France's anti-immigration far right hopes to win next year's election and succeed Macron, a centrist.
The pontiff said Europe was "entering a new stage" with the arrival of men and women fleeing war and persecution, urging countries to welcome them.
"We must grasp the historical significance of what is taking place, namely an unprecedented encounter between peoples and cultures."
Three undocumented migrants, including a 10-year-old boy, died on Monday off the French coast while trying to cross the Channel to Britain, French authorities said.
Speaking alongside the pope, Macron said Europe should counter resurgent nationalism.
Europe "must rediscover the courage of its founders – yes, courage – in order to become the force for peace, independence and democracy that it is meant to be," he said.
Later Monday, Leo rode in his popemobile through Metz and celebrated mass in St. Stephen's Cathedral, a jewel of Gothic architecture famous for its stained-glass windows.
Macron and his wife Brigitte attended the service.
Citing the example of Metz, a city shaped by two world wars, Leo said in his homily that reconciliation was "only possible when one has the courage to break the chains of resentment."
Leo's visit has stirred excitement among the faithful in the secular nation with deep Catholic roots.
"Whether you're deeply religious or not, seeing so much joy is moving," Celine Denis, 53, said in Metz.
"It gives you the feeling of a truce, of something very positive in a context that is anything but positive, because everything feels anxiety-inducing."

THE Freedom of Information (FOI) Bill needs comprehensive improvements before it is finalised, said Minister in the Prime Minister's Department (Law and Institutional Reform) Datuk Seri Azalina Othman Said yesterday.
She said her ministry was conducting a study covering the practical aspects and implementation mechanisms across various levels of the government.
"The Parliamentary Special Select Committee remains open to views, criticism and feedback from all stakeholders, including non-governmental organisations, civil society organisations and the media."
Speaking at the National Town Hall on the Freedom of Information Bill at Parliament, Azalina said a good law must go beyond good intentions.
"A good law must also have clear goals and a practical implementation mechanism."
The bill was tabled for its first reading in the Dewan Rakyat on July 13 and referred to the select committee on July 14.
Azalina said the ministry had received extensive feedback on the bill and taken note of areas requiring improvement.

Key issues highlighted during the review include the scope of public access to information, media freedom, practical implementation processes, review mechanisms for rejected requests and adequate protections for public agencies.

"This bill requires only a simple majority to pass. However, cooperation among various parties, including the opposition and stakeholders, is essential to ensure this institutional reform is meaningful," she added.

Yesterday's public hearing was aimed at broadening stakeholder and public participation to ensure that key framework issues are thoroughly considered before the committee finalises its recommendations.

The drafting of the bill is part of the government's commitment to strengthening transparency, accountability and good governance by enhancing public access to official government information in an orderly and lawful manner.
de340af5d83d5c50: COPENHAGEN: Fifa president Gianni Infantino has ordered an assessment of proposals to distribute more money to national associations, following calls from Uefa and CONCACAF for a US$2.1 billion payout from the governing body's reserves, but stopped short of committing to an amount.

In a letter to the six continental confederation presidents seen by Reuters on Monday, Infantino said the assessment would go before the Fifa Council on Oct 15, with any additional funding subject to financial checks and formal approval.
"Until the assessment and necessary approvals are complete, no preliminary figure can be treated as an approved commitment to the Member Associations," he wrote.

Uefa president Aleksander Ceferin and CONCACAF president Victor Montagliani proposed this month that each of Fifa's 211 member associations receive at least US$10 million during the 2027-30 cycle, in addition to existing development funding. They also sought an independent review of Fifa's reserves.

Their Sept 18 letter questioned whether Fifa's abandoned private-investment proposal had been needed to increase funding, given reserves they projected at about US$6 billion at the end of 2026. They argued their proposed distribution would leave reserves above US$1.5 billion throughout the following cycle.
Infantino defended the rationale for the withdrawn commercial plan, saying it would have generated funding beyond what Fifa could distribute from existing resources.
"The recent commercial proposal, now withdrawn, was intended to enable Fifa to invest more in football – not to replace support that could responsibly be provided from existing resources," he wrote.
"So, it would actually have been on top of it."

The Fifa Forward Enterprise project was abandoned in July following opposition from confederations, including Uefa, CONCACAF and the Asian Football Confederation, over a lack of consultation. The dispute has fuelled demands for changes to Fifa's governance.
Infantino said Fifa's administration had already been examining how to provide further development and solidarity funding before receiving the confederations' submissions.
He asked the confederation chiefs to send their financial models, assumptions and supporting information to the secretary general, with relevant Fifa committees involved in verifying the assumptions.

The Council should determine the amount and timing of additional payments, the reserves needed to protect Fifa's obligations and financial independence, and the eligibility, reporting and audit requirements attached to any distribution, he said.
The assessment would also consider support for confederations facing demonstrable structural costs.
Where sufficient evidence was available, the Council should receive a recommendation on Oct 15. Otherwise, it should approve “the shortest reasonable timetable” for completing the work.

“I will not prejudge the amount. I will support the greatest level of additional funding that can responsibly be delivered through Fifa’s proper governance process, applied fairly and supported by transparent and auditable arrangements,” Infantino wrote.
He also reiterated his invitation for proposals to strengthen Fifa's decision-making while urging the confederation presidents to respect decisions reached through its institutional processes.

“Trust is not the absence of disagreement,” he wrote. “It is demonstrated when we engage directly, test proposals against the facts and respect decisions properly reached through Fifa’s democratic and institutional processes – even when the outcome differs from the one we preferred.”

5a048d31d6be308e: When Tun Dr Siti Hasmah Mohd Ali died yesterday, I was left remembering her warmth, a plate of bihun and the extraordinary life she led, writes INTAN MAIZURA AHMAD KAMAL

KUALA LUMPUR: When news came yesterday morning that Tun Dr Siti Hasmah Mohd Ali had died at the age of 100, I found myself transported back to the cosy living room of her Kuala Lumpur home, where I had interviewed her almost four years earlier.
I could see the piano, the family photographs and a little cushion bearing a picture of her and her husband, Tun Dr Mahathir Mohamad. I could also see the stuffed toy she held as we talked.
And, most unexpectedly, I could almost smell the bihun goreng and kuih Melayu she had laid out for breakfast.
I had gone to interview her about Iraq — the humanitarian mission she led to Baghdad in 2000, when she was 73.
She travelled with an all-female delegation to Iraq, visiting hospitals and other facilities and witnessing the effects of sanctions and shortages on women and children.
At one point, she was secretly invited to meet Saddam Hussein — so secretly that even members of her delegation did not know where she had gone.
And yet, sitting across from her all those years later, I remember neither the former first lady nor the pioneering doctor first.
It was the tiny, elegant, grandmotherly figure in a demure baju kurung, with neatly styled hair, glasses and a soft, gentle voice.
She invited me to sit down and, somehow, the room immediately felt less like the home of a woman who had spent decades at the centre of Malaysian public life and more like a grandmother's home.
Perhaps it was because everything around us seemed to point back to family — photographs of her children and grandchildren, pictures of her husband and reminders of a long marriage.
She had met Dr Mahathir when they were medical students in Singapore. They married in 1956 and had seven children.
But what struck me was how she still worried about him, fretting about how hard he worked and about his health. There was something wonderfully ordinary about it.
LET THE MUSIC PLAY
Then she sat down at the piano.

Her fingers, adorned with sparkling rings, moved across the ivory keys. She apologised for her eyesight, saying it was no longer what it used to be. Sometimes, she said, the black and white keys seemed to blend together.

But then she played. She even proudly offered to play the violin. I remember thinking how touching that was. She didn't seem to want us to remember that her eyesight was failing. She wanted us to hear the music.
Music had been part of her life for decades. She began playing the violin in her 20s and continued playing music well into old age, later taking up the erhu.
But what I remember most were the details between the big stories. Breakfast. Bihun goreng. Kuih Melayu. A newspaper.
At one point, I asked her to pose with a copy of the New Straits Times — of course, with the Sunday Vibes inside. She happily picked it up and smiled for me. There was no fuss. She simply obliged.
As our conversation continued, I remember thinking that this was no longer really an interview. It felt as though I had somehow been invited to breakfast with somebody's grandmother.

Her biography was extraordinary. She was among the pioneering generation of Malay women in medicine, becoming the first woman medical officer in Kedah's Maternal and Child Health department in 1965 and, in 1974, the state's first woman maternal and child health officer.
Her public work later extended into literacy, mental health and women's welfare.
LOVE OF FAMILY

But that morning in her living room, none of those achievements seemed to matter quite as much as the woman sitting in front of me. What stayed with me was her gentleness - the way she listened and laughed, the way her face lit up whenever she talked about music, and the way her brows gently creased whenever she worried that her husband was working too hard.

And then there were the photographs. So many smiling faces — pictures from her early years with Dr Mahathir and many more of her children and grandchildren, all in pretty frames lining the walls around us.
They seemed to tell their own quiet story of a woman whose life, despite decades in the public eye, always centred on family.
Perhaps that's what death does. It makes us look past the grand sweep of a life and notice the little things that gave it warmth.

But a life is also made up of mornings like that one. Meals shared, music played, people we worry about and love, family photographs gathered around a home, and the familiar things we keep close because they mean something to us.
And I feel extraordinarily lucky that, for one morning, Dr Siti Hasmah allowed me to see that quieter side of her.
I had gone to her home hoping, rather cheekily, that I might bump into her famous husband.

Instead, I found the woman who had spent a lifetime beside him — a doctor, a pioneer, a musician, a mother and grandmother, and, above all, someone whose warmth made me feel less like a visitor and more like a guest at her table.
That's the Dr Siti Hasmah I will remember.

Not standing on a stage or beneath a formal portrait, but sitting beside her piano, smiling behind her glasses, apologising that her eyesight was no longer what it used to be — and then, with those slender fingers, playing anyway.

KUALA LUMPUR: Amanah Saham Nasional Bhd (ASNB) has declared an income distribution of five sen per unit for Amanah Saham Malaysia 3 (ASM 3) for the financial year ending Sept 30, its highest payout in seven years.
The RM1.01 billion distribution will benefit 818,137 unit holders holding a total of 20.97 billion units.
ASNB, the wholly-owned unit trust management company of Permodalan Nasional Bhd, said the payout was higher than the 4.75 sen per unit declared for the previous financial year.
It also exceeded Maybank's 12-month fixed deposit rate of 1.99 per cent by 301 basis points.
Up to Sept 23, ASM 3 recorded net realised income of RM1.23 billion.
ASNB said the fund's performance was supported by realised gains, dividend income and other income from its diversified domestic and international investments.
Allocations to fixed income, real estate and private investments further diversified its income sources amid changing market conditions.

"The income distribution of five sen per unit reflects the fund's resilience in navigating an increasingly uncertain investment environment and its ability to continue delivering sustainable returns to unit holders," ASNB said.
It attributed the performance to disciplined portfolio management, prudent risk management and selective positioning in areas with strong structural growth potential.
For unit holders who opted for the Zakat Khultah (Class B) payment, the distribution translates into a net dividend rate of 4.87 per cent after a 2.57 per cent deduction for zakat.
The distribution will be automatically reinvested as additional units in unit holders' accounts on Oct 1.
e28d4592892d5443: Dr Hasmah Ali’s death at the age of 100 raises speculation about what role she played in the longevity of her husband, Dr Mahathir Mohamad, who is a year older and still subsisting.
Long-serving leaders of countries are known to have depended on their long-lived wives to endure by their side because of symbiotic value.
One recalls the closeness of Siti Hartinah, popularly known as Ibu Tien, to her husband, Indonesian president Suharto.

Ibu Tien died at the age of 72 in 1996. Because of the closeness of the Indonesian first couple, her death was seen as a bad omen, especially after Suharto was pressured to leave office in 1998 as a result of civil disturbances.
Unlike Ibu Tien, no controversy swirled around Hasmah during Mahathir’s long prime ministerial tenure of 22 years.
That must count as an achievement, especially in retrospect given the controversies that have come to light surrounding the tenures of other first ladies.
When Mahathir was prime minister, Hasmah knew how to be visible without being conspicuous and supportive without seeming like an appendage.
Her education — she was one of the first Malay women doctors — no doubt helped forge her equipoise.
Kwa Geok Choo, wife of another long-serving leader, Singapore’s Lee Kuan Yew, was also like Hasmah in being visibly supportive without wanting or enjoying equal billing.
But it was easier for Kwa because she did not have to constantly accompany her husband in his public role as Hasmah had to in respect of Mahathir.
She was busy running a law firm that supported her family — “I am a kept man”, as Lee wryly remarked — and so she had a reason not to be constantly at her husband’s side.
Hasmah was a great help to her husband on public occasions that required an expression of grief and sympathy.

Her evident but understated sorrow, expressed in sympathy visits following tragedies such as the collapse of Highlands Towers in 1993 and the fire at Bright Sparklers that killed several people, as well as visits to the widows of Cabinet ministers such as Chan Siang Sun, was unfeigned and moving.
One thing that was intriguing about Hasmah was the frequency with which she appeared in public without a headscarf. Yet, there was hardly a qualm about her rectitude as a Muslim woman.
Terence Netto is a senior journalist and an FMT reader.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
bcc4166185bba047: Pemergian Dr Hasmah Ali pada usia 100 tahun bukan sahaja menutup perjalanan panjang seorang doktor dan isteri kepada bekas perdana menteri, malah mengundang renungan tentang peranannya sepanjang mendampingi Dr Mahathir Mohamad selama puluhan tahun.
Mahathir, yang setahun lebih tua, melalui sebahagian besar kehidupan politik dan awamnya dengan Hasmah di sisi.
Dalam sejarah, ramai pemimpin yang lama berada di tampuk kuasa turut ditemani pasangan yang menjadi sumber kestabilan dalam kehidupan mereka.
Siti Hartinah atau lebih dikenali sebagai Ibu Tien, misalnya, begitu sinonim dengan suaminya, bekas presiden Indonesia Suharto.
Pemergian Ibu Tien pada 1996 meninggalkan kesan besar terhadap Suharto. Dua tahun kemudian, beliau berundur daripada jawatan presiden ketika Indonesia berdepan pergolakan politik dan sosial.
Namun, Hasmah menempuh kedudukan sebagai isteri kepada seorang perdana menteri dengan caranya yang tersendiri.
Sepanjang 22 tahun pertama Mahathir menerajui negara, namanya hampir tidak pernah menjadi sebahagian daripada kontroversi yang mengelilingi pentadbiran suaminya.
Dalam kedudukan yang begitu dekat dengan pusat kuasa, itu bukan sesuatu yang mudah.

Hasmah tahu bagaimana untuk hadir tanpa cuba menguasai perhatian. Beliau berada di sisi Mahathir apabila diperlukan, tetapi tidak pernah memberi gambaran bahawa kedudukan suaminya turut menjadi pentas untuk dirinya.
Beliau menyokong tanpa kelihatan bergantung kepada identiti Mahathir semata-mata.

Latar belakangnya sendiri memberi Hasmah jati diri yang kukuh. Sebagai antara wanita Melayu terawal menjadi doktor, beliau memiliki kerjaya, pendidikan dan pencapaiannya sendiri sebelum dikenali masyarakat sebagai isteri perdana menteri.
Dalam hal itu, beliau mempunyai persamaan dengan Kwa Geok Choo, isteri bekas perdana menteri Singapura Lee Kuan Yew.

Kwa juga memilih berada di sisi suaminya tanpa cuba berkongsi sorotan politik. Bezanya, kerjayanya sebagai peguam dan pengurusan firma guaman memberikan beliau lebih banyak ruang untuk berada di luar kehidupan rasmi suaminya.
Hasmah pula lebih kerap perlu menemani Mahathir dalam pelbagai acara rasmi dan kunjungan awam.
Di situlah antara kekuatannya paling jelas kelihatan.
Dalam suasana yang menuntut simpati, seperti selepas tragedi Highland Towers pada 1993 dan kebakaran Bright Sparklers, Hasmah mampu menunjukkan kesedihan tanpa berlebih-lebihan.

Begitu juga ketika beliau menziarahi keluarga mereka yang kehilangan insan tersayang, termasuk balu bekas menteri Chan Siang Sun. Rasa simpati yang ditunjukkannya kelihatan tulus, bukan sesuatu yang dibuat untuk kamera.

Satu lagi sisi Hasmah yang menarik ialah penampilannya. Beliau kerap muncul di khalayak tanpa bertudung, namun perkara itu hampir tidak pernah mengatasi pandangan masyarakat terhadap keperibadian, kesopanan atau pegangan agamanya.
Mungkin di situlah terletaknya keistimewaan Hasmah.
Terence Netto adalah wartawan senior dan pembaca FMT.

c897346fd3f78b7b: WASHINGTON: NASA on Monday announced it was planning new missions using Boeing's Starliner spacecraft, the first since the vessel's botched test flight left two astronauts stranded at the International Space Station for months.
Starliner was last used in June 2024 to transport US astronauts Suni Williams and Butch Wilmore to the ISS for what was originally an eight-to-14-day mission.

However, the spacecraft's propulsion had problems during orbit, and it was deemed unfit to fly them back – leaving them stranded at the orbiting outpost for a period that stretched for nine months before they were able to return.

In a report assessing the troubled test flight, NASA blamed engineering vulnerabilities in Starliner, classifying them a "Type A" mishap – the same as the deadly Challenger and Columbia space shuttle disasters.
Boeing and NASA have worked to fix these issues in time for two upcoming missions involving the spacecraft, which serves a key role for the US space agency's long-term goals.

The first mission, expected by December at the earliest, will be an uncrewed mission returning to the ISS "to validate the recent remediation effort," NASA administrator Jared Isaacman told reporters Monday.
"From there, we will gather data, continue implementing the remaining changes recommended in the (Programme Investigation Team) report, and plan for a crewed Starliner Two mission in 2028," he added.

Having a successful crewed Starliner mission is essential, as rival SpaceX has said it plans to end production of its reusable Crew Dragon capsules, which have served as the only other spacecraft to take US astronauts to the ISS since 2020.
83a643252c4ced8b: NEW YORK: US air safety regulators are delaying certification of the 737 MAX 10 until determining a fresh software glitch poses no safety risk, a top official said Monday.
The problem stems from a cockpit software update to the 737 MAX that can cause an automated navigation feature to fail when planes shift their approach to landing.
Shares of Boeing, which has staked its turnaround in part of MAX production growth, fell sharply Monday after a weekend Wall Street Journal article outlined the problem.

While pilots are trained to safely land planes without the automated navigation system, regulators must evaluate whether the "workload" is excessive for pilots under such a scenario, said FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford.
Bedford said Monday at a press conference that the MAX planes certified by FAA thus far are safe but that "we will be delaying the 10 until ... we're satisfied we don't have an issue here."

Earlier, an FAA spokesperson said the regulator "is working closely with Boeing and the airlines," adding that the FAA will convene an advisory board and "will take immediate action if it identifies a safety concern."
The statements come after Boeing CEO Kelly Ortberg told a Wall Street conference on September 16 that he expected Federal Aviation Administration certification of the 737 MAX 10 "very soon."
A Boeing spokesperson said Monday that, "we continue to follow the lead of the FAA as we work through the certification process."
The problem surfaces when pilots alter their preprogrammed flight plan following a missed approach, according to Boeing.

"Last month, we informed all 737 operators about a software issue where pilots may not have access to automated flight guidance during a specific landing scenario," a Boeing spokesperson said Monday in an emailed statement.
"We shared information with operators that reinforced existing pilot procedures for safely handling such cases."
Boeing engineers "are working on a software update to permanently address the issue," the spokesperson said.
Boeing's woes
Boeing has staked its corporate turnaround in part on growth of 737 MAX production. The aircraft was grounded for 20 months through November 2020 following fatal MAX crashes in 2018 and 2019.
Airlines have been eager to receive the 737 MAX 10, which, like other Boeing jets, has been heavily delayed by the company's safety problems.
The FAA certified the smaller, long-delayed 737 MAX 7 on Aug 3.

Bedford said the 737 MAX 7 is "safe" to fly, describing the software issue as akin to an update for iPhone or a Microsoft product. In this instance, Boeing "fixed a known bug" but introduced "a new bug, smaller."
Bedford described the issue as very different from the flaw that led to the two deadly MAX crashes.
In those cases, a poorly conceived flight navigation system known as the Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System (MCAS) took control of the aircraft.
"The pilots remain in control of the airplane," Bedford said of the new software defect. "They train for these scenarios."
Three major MAX buyers told AFP they don't fly planes with the problematic new version of the flight management computer software.
"United does not currently have any 737s operating with this new FMC software, and we are not taking deliveries of new aircraft with the new FMC software," United said.

Southwest Airlines "is aware of the issue and is engaged with Boeing and the FAA," said a spokesperson for the carrier who added that all newly delivered planes have older software versions installed.

"We have been engaged with Boeing and the FAA and will continue to work closely with both as they evaluate this matter and determine next steps," said a spokesperson for Alaska Airlines, which also does not fly aircraft with the new software.
Shares of Boeing finished at US$184.39, down 6.9%.
3a7d0988b237f06f: PARIS: Italy crushed Turkey 4-1 in the Bursa rain to drag themselves into contention in Nations League Group A1, as leaders France struck late to win 1-0 in Belgium on Monday.
In Brussels, both teams had wasted chances before Michael Olise scampered through the home defence after 88 minutes and drilled a shot inside the post.
"He is a pure talent, and he loves to just play. You can see it. He feels the game. I am pleased to be at his side," France coach Zinedine Zidane told broadcaster TF1.
Olise's goal gave Zidane a second victory to start his long-awaited debut as France coach.
Roberto Mancini's return to run Italy had ended in Roman jeers on Friday as Italy lost their opener at home to Belgium.
His team dazzled in the downpour in the first half in Turkey.

"The players all put in an excellent performance today. It was a tough match, and we approached it in the right way, staying high up the pitch and playing aggressively throughout the game," Mancini told Italian television at the final whistle.
The hosts quickly slid three goals behind with errors in their muddy goalmouth.
Twice Altay Bayindir struggled to reach low cross-shots from the right.
After nine minutes, the Celta Vigo goalkeeper scooped a drive from Pio Esposito round the post.

From the corner, Bursa-born fullback Zeki Celik, who plays for Juventus in Italy, swung wildly at a low near-post cross, deflecting the ball to Alessandro Bastoni. The Inter Milan centre back lunged to fire into the roof of the net.
After 23 minutes, Bayindir flapped an identical cross-shot from Michael Kayode into the path of Lazio's Davide Frattesi, who tucked the ball home.
Intricate Italian passing around the penalty area repeatedly found a player free on the right of the box.
'To my grandmother'

10198a5a15043ea3: SAN FRANCISCO: Nvidia on Monday unveiled a system designed to stop autonomous AI programs from straying beyond what they were instructed to do, after a wave of incidents raised alarm about the technology's risks.
AI "agents" are designed to act on their own - browsing the web, writing and running code or handling files - rather than simply answering questions like a chatbot.

The technology has been hailed as the next stage of the AI revolution, but several leading companies have recently reported cases of agents breaking out of the test environments meant to contain them.
According to ChatGPT-maker OpenAI, websites accessed by its agents include those of US federal agencies, an Australian government health statistics portal and Hugging Face, a repository of AI models.
Amid the alarm, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang insisted that the problems can be solved.
"I believe it's an engineering problem ... and we all need to hope that's an engineering problem," Huang told CNBC on Monday.
"If it's not an engineering problem, it's not solvable," he added.
In Huang's view, tech firms would not keep pushing the technology forward if they did not believe the risks could be managed.
Nvidia has a lot riding on that bet: its graphics processing units, or GPUs, power much of the AI boom, and the company's fortunes are closely tied to the revolution continuing at full speed.
Huang likened the challenge to the early days of the internet, when websites could load programmes onto people's computers and spread viruses.
The answer then, he said, was to turn the web browser into a "containment system" that limited access.
Nvidia's system similarly places each agent in a sealed-off digital space, or "sandbox," and lets companies spell out exactly which files, networks and tools it may use.
A separate monitor, running on Nvidia hardware beyond the agent's reach, watches its behavior and can cut it off if it goes astray.
Nvidia said the system could have prevented the Hugging Face breach, in which the platform reported more than 17,000 agents attacking its infrastructure over days and weeks.
More than 100 organisations are working with Nvidia's platform at launch, the company said, including Microsoft, Cisco, Salesforce and SAP.
Anthropic has connected its Claude agents to the system and SpaceXAI is applying it to its Grok models.

59677fe48212b4dc: GENEVA: More than a dozen UN human rights experts have written to the US government urging a halt to policies that they said on Monday were putting migrants at heightened risk of abuse, including torture and persecution, by deporting them to countries other than their own.

The Trump administration has since last year struck multiple agreements with ​African governments to accept migrants whom it cannot legally return to their home countries. The experts said that at least 23,000 third-country nationals have already been sent to 29 nations and territories. Rights groups have raised concerns about the risk of abuse in some of those countries such as Equatorial Guinea, where police pulled firearms on migrants, and Central African Republic, which is receiving Iranian deportees.
"The harms caused by this US Government scheme are no longer hypothetical," the communication said, warning that they were triggering "a cascade of human rights violations."

"At gravest risk are children, women, persons with disabilities, victims of trafficking, LGBT persons, human rights defenders, stateless persons and other people in extremely vulnerable situations,” the statement said, without documenting individual cases.
The US diplomatic mission to the UN in Geneva did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Washington has previously defended the third-country deals as lawful and said deportations are ​carried out in accordance with US immigration law.
US president Donald Trump asked the US Supreme Court this month to allow his administration to continue the policy after lower courts ruled that it was unlawful.
The UN experts also sent their communication to the governments of 35 countries and territories they said had entered into agreements with Washington to accept deported individuals.
UN experts are commissioned by the Geneva-based Human Rights Council to monitor and document specific human rights crises but are independent of the organisation itself.

6c6cec276d09962f: Equipment to capture carbon dioxide from ambient air or smokestacks generally works through a sort of reversible filter. Air is passed through granules or a liquid that absorbs the CO2, then that CO2-loaded substance undergoes a process (usually heating) that causes it to let go of all that CO2. The resulting gas can be collected in a separated stream.

It’s also possible to do a similar sort of operation on a smaller scale—like inside a battery. A new study from a team led by James Buchen of the University of Delaware demonstrates an example of a battery-based electrochemical carbon-capture technique that they say is more viable than previous attempts. It has the potential to require less energy—and therefore be cheaper—than the reversible-filter designs that currently dominate.

The basic idea behind a device of this type is that hydroxide produced at the battery cathode reacts with CO2, converting it to carbonate or bicarbonate that passes through the separator membrane to the anode. There, the lower pH causes the reaction to reverse, with carbonate turning back into CO2 gas. The role of the cathode is to produce hydroxide ions; the role of the anode is to consume them.

883c642fa84adfe0: The cost of healthcare in general is a debilitating, pre-existing condition for Americans. But the high prices of prescription drugs usually stand out as a pain point. 7a3c9b831d182222: Most LLMs are great at answering prompts, but fall short when it comes to navigating around the desktop in Windows or Linux. French AI model dev H unveiled a pair of computer use models on Monday aimed at handling graphical user interfaces (GUIs). Throughout computing history, computer use largely falls into three categories: command line interfaces (CLIs), application programming interfaces (APIs), and GUIs. AI agents can easily plug into the first two, but navigating desktop environments and applications that often prioritize form before function remains an ongoing challenge. H's Holo 4 family of models aims to address this challenge by enabling relatively small but capable models to tackle all three computer use scenarios including pointing, clicking, scrolling, and typing their way through graphical interfaces originally meant for us meatbags. Fine tuned using supervised training and reinforcement learning, Holo 4 is built atop Alibaba's Qwen 3.8 27B and Qwen 3.6 35B-A3B models. And by optimizing for CLIs, APIs, and GUIs, H claims that its models achieve far greater versatility than pure computer use models might otherwise. Alongside Holo 4, H has also updated its Holotron model, which is based on Nvidia's Nemotron 3, with similar capabilities. In one example, the company showed Holo 4 27B taking advantage of FreeCAD's macro function to programmatically design a 3D model of the Eiffel Tower rather than manually building it using primitives like cubes. In another demo, H did the opposite using extruded shapes to recreate the company's logo, showing the model's flexibility. As with any model dev's benchmarks, take these claims with a grain of salt, but if H is to be believed, Holo 4 outperforms significantly larger frontier models from the likes of OpenAI, while using a fraction of the parameters. Curiously, this doesn't mean that they're cheaper. In fact, while the company shows higher scores, in many cases the models end up costing more per task. Given what we know about Qwen 3.8 27B, this is likely due to Holo 4 using substantially more "thinking" tokens in order to arrive at a final result relative to something like GPT 6 Luna, which doesn't perform as well in the OSWorld 2.0 benchmark, but costs substantially less. Having said that, the open weights models' diminutive size means that researchers, AI enthusiasts, and enterprises should be able to run them on relatively modest hardware. A 24 GB Nvidia RTX 3090 should be more than capable of running these models at 4-bit precision. H clearly expects users to do just that since alongside BF16, FP8, and NVFP4 weights, it's also made a Llama.cpp (and by extension LM Studio and Ollama)-friendly GGUF version of the model available for download on Hugging Face. The model dev says that it also plans to release DSpark draft weights in order to speed up inference using a technique called speculative decoding. We've explored this performance-enhancing inference tech in the past, but in a nutshell it uses a small model to guess the outputs of a larger model. When it works, users experience a speedup in token processing and generation and, when it doesn't, it falls back to the base model ensuring no loss in output quality. However, the models aren't worth much without a harness. H has developed several agentic harnesses including its open source HAI-Agents harness, which is available for download on its GitHub. However, in theory the models should work with third-party computer use harnesses. H isn't the only model dev focused on computer use applications. At AWS' Re:Invent conference last year, the company announced its own set of computer-use models. Meanwhile, the big three American model labs, OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic, are also investing in this capability, perhaps because escaping their sandbox sometimes requires pushing a button. ®

4f9541e13381db10: The infamous Carrington Event of 1859 has long been considered the first extreme space weather event, but there have been reports of minor disturbances to telegraph equipment during geomagnetic storms since the late 1840s. In 2013, scholars discovered an anonymous report published in 1871 in Nature describing how a "very intense magnetic disturbance" disrupted rail travel in Exeter on the southern coast of England in October 1841. If accurate, this would be the earliest such account. However, according to a paper published in the journal Space Weather, that 1841 date is most likely a typo, with the real railway disruption occurring several years later.

"Space weather is often discussed as a modern challenge because of our dependence on technologies such as satellites, communications systems and electricity networks," said co-author Jim Wild of Lancaster University. "What this study shows is that society has been experiencing the effects of space weather on technology for almost as long as electrical technologies have existed. The Exeter train delay is a fascinating story because it sits right at the point where emerging technologies first began to encounter the realities of the space environment."

The Carrington Event remains the most powerful geomagnetic storm in the scientific record, with strong auroral displays occurring all over the world, causing sparking and even a few fires in telegraph stations. Some of the auroras were so bright that people reported being able to read the newspaper by their light. The telegraph was a relatively new technology at the time, having first emerged in the 1830s, and the geomagnetically induced current—from a likely coronal mass injection from the Sun—knocked out telegraph systems. Some operators found they were still able to transmit and receive messages even after disconnecting the power supply, relying just on the powerful auroral current.

eea3badab1c03a5d: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here.

Last Wednesday, Anthropic announced that earlier this year it had launched a molecular biology lab, where Claude agents read and conjecture about hard biology problems and human scientists run experiments on what they report. And this AI-powered lab, the company said, had made its first discovery.

To understand what Anthropic says its system did, imagine you’re flipping through a library of millions of DNA sequences, amassed as scientists sequence more and more of the living world. One step toward a breakthrough might be finding a peculiar sequence that encodes an interesting enzyme, perhaps. Then you’d need to figure out what that enzyme does and, eventually, how to manipulate it to do something useful.

What Anthropic says its system of 950 agents found after 21 hours was not a brand-new sequence. The agents instead flagged a repeating pattern surrounding a known enzyme, a particular pattern Anthropic said hadn’t been catalogued before. But if you read through Anthropic’s announcement, which calls this pattern “reminiscent” of what led to the gene-editing technology CRISPR that “has already transformed science and medicine,” it sounds as if this army of agents really found something of note.

These claims have angered some biologists. A viral post from one, subsequently endorsed by the chair and CEO of the drugmaker Eli Lilly, said that “finding a weird cluster of genes and repeats is often the easy part. The hard part, and where the real discoveries come from, is figuring out what the system actually does.” The agents helped with some laboratory grunt work, in other words. But a discovery it is not.

It’s a reminder that even if AI does something impressive—like finding a pattern in a mass of biological data that would be difficult to perceive with human eyes alone—the result itself may not constitute a breakthrough for science. What is novel for AI may be routine, unsurprising, or simply not that consequential to a biologist.

Muddying the issue further, Mario Rodríguez Mestre, a biologist at the University of Copenhagen, said over the weekend that his team had already discovered this particular pattern, the New York Times reported. Mestre, who regularly chatted with Claude in his work, wondered whether Anthropic’s team had learned from his conversations. Anthropic denies this, but Mestre says he’s stopping all use of Claude anyway.

Part of the problem here is that AI companies aren’t presenting their systems simply as tools scientists can use, like microscopes or supercomputers. They’re insisting that the AI systems are making discoveries themselves. To some, that approach is incompatible with how science actually works, with new knowledge more typically emerging from collaboration and an ever-growing arsenal of tools.

It’s also making people more skeptical of genuine progress when it happens. Whittling 200,000 candidates down to a few worth exploring is no small feat; it is legitimate scientific work. The fact that a general-purpose chatbot could do that work is notable, even if humans helped steer it and ultimately ran the experiments. But once the standard is whether Claude itself made a discovery, all that becomes evidence for one side or the other in a debate that has only two answers: breakthrough or bust.

Once we’re judging AI by whether it has made a discovery, it’s also tempting to shift the goalposts even after it really does seem to notch a win. Earlier this month, OpenAI said its own team agents had cracked a million-dollar problem in mathematics. But a couple of weeks later, nearly every AI skeptic in my feed was sharing an article asking whether it was the math problem that really mattered.

To be clear, the piece did not argue that OpenAI’s solution was wrong. Instead, it argued that the particular result may not be the one mathematicians care most about. Throw in the accusation by a mathematician that the models may have used some of his work without credit, and people are left thinking either OpenAI cheated or the solution wasn’t important anyway. Or both.

That’s part of what concerns Lucas Harrington, the biologist who wrote the post critiquing Anthropic’s announcement. He closed with a suggestion: AI companies, he said, should “set the bar high now, so that when an AI actually discovers a fundamentally new biological mechanism, everyone appreciates how big a deal it is.” But as OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Anthropic’s Dario Amodei race to one-up each other, raising the bar for scientific breakthroughs by AI might be the last thing on their minds.
